rv.q: Out of this curious quartet, Auburn creates emotionally and intellectually enveloping music.
Together, Bryggman and Parker hit enough emotional highs to sustain a dozen lesser plays.

As directed by Daniel Sullivan and performed by an exemplary cast, ''Proof'' has the pace of a psychological thriller, and if its resolution tilts toward the sentimental, the characters deserve to be hopeful.
It's also rather shallow, the jokes about prime numbers notwithstanding.

It's been a long time since Broadway has seen the debut of a new play the quality of Proof, and even longer since it has welcomed the debut of a new playwright as talented and promising as David Auburn.
Elegance -- and eloquence -- also describe the production as a whole.

Yet Auburn, in his first Broadway outing, provides characters behaving credibly and natural dialogue without a single stagy phrase stumbling the flow and also ensures the tension is handsomely sustained.
Neither will David Auburn’s light but smart play.
I wish I could tell you why that play is among the best of the season—but believe me, it truly is.

cn.t: Critics praise Auburn's compelling mystery-drama for its accessible storytelling and Mary-Louise Parker's thrilling performance, though some dismiss it as a highbrow soap opera with superficial nods to mathematics.
